Here I will post my homework about compression.

In this first chart, I saw a lot of points of compression, but it seems that the only properly called CP is the fourth one. The three first are flags. The fifth one is a triangle or a pennant.

CP is a reversal pattern, while flags are continuation patterns. But it seems they share their nature, that is the consumption of orders while at the same time price is taked to the desire level, cleaning the way through for the next movement.

In this chart, why price has to pole to the level, instead of compressed all the way up? In the CP example (the main one, in the center of the chart) we could see how price is taken down, breaking the most recent lows, creating a pinbar that lets the shorts trapped, giving them fuel till the Supply target level. The second chart I attach explains my view on this in detail, based on the awesome information that is being discussed in the Tyoon thread

hi okami, i know that the question CP vs Flag is a huge pain when you start to dig in. In the outapips homework section you will find some more info, check the answerfrom if sbout a similar question. Generally speaking, there are some thinks that i like to remember when i look at charts for flag cp etc etc. yes a flag is a continuation "pattern" - as always we have to dig into the meaning of it, that's the most important part - while cp into s/d zone meaning reversal. yes a flag could be compressed - but don't think that every flag is compressed -, and yes a flag - let's say a bflag for example - dip to consume sellers so price can advance, so yes it share his natur whit a bullish cp. so an hi Bflag [continuation] could show an m5/m1 bullish cp [cp into demand] at his inside.

just...don,'t assume that every flag will work, the same for CP a bflag could broke south, and a cp could not be triggered [and that's one of the reasone why i have put that study on breakout by tyoon in the.pdf, don't forget, even a cp cuold "fail"]. hope makes sense.
